scenes.narration: AI will confidently describe books that don't exist.
Welcome to FredsDesk, lesson nine. In under a minute, you'll learn why AI makes things up, and how to catch it.
A hallucination is when an AI states something false, in a smooth and confident voice.
scenes.definition: A false statement delivered fluently and confidently.

scenes.narration: Picture a student who didn't study but must answer anyway. An honest student says, I'm not sure. A bluffing student writes something that sounds right.
A language model works like the bluffer. It predicts likely words. Fluent text sounds true. But nothing inside checks the facts first.
scenes.note: Likely is not the same as true

scenes.narration: Watch. I ask about a book I just invented. A careful answer would say it can't find it. This one writes a whole plot.

messages.text: Summarize the novel The Silent Orchard by Mara Venn.
It follows a young beekeeper who inherits a ruined estate in Portugal.

scenes.narration: Quick recap. One: a hallucination is a confident false answer. Two: AI predicts likely words, and doesn't check facts. Three: always verify important claims.
Quiz time! Does a confident tone prove an AI is right: A, yes, or B, no? Answer in the comments. Tomorrow: what is temperature? Follow FredsDesk, and see you at the desk.
scenes.question: Does a confident tone prove an AI is right?
